title: Voltage Divider Design and Validation
purpose: Create a passive output voltage lower than an input voltage using two resistors while accounting for load current and source loading.
whenToUse: bias generation where load impedance is high
whenNotToUse: Power regulation
low-impedance loads
precision references without buffering or tolerance analysis

parameters.vout: target unloaded or loaded output voltage

designEquations: unloaded: vout = vin * r2 / (r1 + r2)
loaded: r2eff = 1 / (1/r2 + 1/rLoad); vout = vin * r2eff / (r1 + r2eff)
input current = vin / (r1 + r2eff)
designProcedure: Decide allowable divider current versus load current.
Choose rTotal so divider current is usually at least 10x load current when accuracy matters.
Calculate r2 = rTotal * vout / vin and r1 = rTotal - r2 for unloaded case, or solve loaded equation when load is known.
Select practical resistor values and estimate tolerance error.
Construct the divider and load in the schematic.
Run operating-point analysis or DC sweep.
Measure vout and source current.
analysisRecipe: Run ERC before solver analysis.
Run operating point for nominal vout.
Run DC sweep if input range matters.
Run tolerance or worst-case analysis when precision matters.
validationCriteria: Vout within specified tolerance under load.
Divider current and resistor power below limits.
Source loading acceptable.
iterationRules: Lower resistor values or add a buffer if loading error is excessive.
Use precision resistors or a reference/regulator if tolerance error is excessive.
capabilityGaps: General operating-point and DC sweep execution are not yet fully exposed as reusable agent tools in the prototype.
text: Recipe: Voltage divider. Use for low-current scaling or biasing, not for power regulation or low-impedance loads. Equations: unloaded vout = vin*r2/(r1+r2); loaded use r2eff = r2 || rLoad. Procedure: choose divider current, compute R1/R2, place source/resistors/load/ground, run ERC, run operating point or DC sweep, verify vout/current/power/tolerance. Failure modes: load too low, tolerance, power, false-regulator use. Capability gap: general operating-point/DC sweep is not yet a reusable agent tool.

title: First-Order RC Low-Pass Filter
purpose: Create a single-pole low-pass response with -3 dB cutoff set by R and C.
whenNotToUse: sharp transition bands
low source impedance into heavy load without buffering
high-precision filters requiring controlled Q
designEquations: fc = 1 / (2*pi*R*C)
C = 1 / (2*pi*R*fc)
loaded response depends on source and load impedances
designProcedure: Choose R based on source/load impedance and acceptable noise/current.
Calculate C from target cutoff.
Select practical C and recompute cutoff.
Construct source, R series, C to ground, and optional load.
Place scope CH1 at output and CH2 at input when comparing response.
Run ERC, then AC sweep.
Measure -3 dB cutoff, passband gain, and rolloff.
analysisRecipe: AC sweep from at least fc/100 to fc*100.
Plot output/input gain from returned numeric vectors.
Confirm approximately -20 dB/decade above cutoff.
validationCriteria: Measured -3 dB frequency within requirement tolerance.
Passband loading acceptable.
Rolloff near -20 dB/decade after the pole.
iterationRules: Adjust C or R and rerun AC sweep.
Add a buffer if load shifts response too much.
capabilityGaps: General AC sweep over arbitrary schematic netlists and vector plotting must be exposed as reusable tools; do not substitute hand-drawn curves.
text: Recipe: RC low-pass filter. Use fc = 1/(2*pi*R*C). Choose R from impedance/noise/current constraints, compute C, build source-R-output-C-ground, run ERC, run AC sweep from fc/100 to fc*100, plot output/input from actual vectors, verify -3 dB cutoff and -20 dB/decade rolloff. Capability gap: arbitrary AC sweep/vector plotting needs reusable tool exposure.

title: Matched Second-Order RLC High-Pass Filter
purpose: Design a passive second-order high-pass section for matched source/load impedance and validate cutoff response from simulated sweep data.
whenToUse: agent validation of AC response workflow
whenNotToUse: high efficiency power filtering without component loss checks
very low cutoff where required inductors/capacitors are impractical
arbitrary impedance transformations
designEquations: omega = 2*pi*fc
Butterworth denominator uses Q = 1/sqrt(2) in normalized voltage transfer form; this app's matched recipe calculates C = 1/(omega*z0*sqrt(2)) and L = z0/(omega*sqrt(2))
source resistor = load resistor = z0
designProcedure: Parse target cutoff and matched impedance.
Use filter_design_high_pass if the request matches the supported matched RLC high-pass recipe.
Verify the generated circuit contains source resistor, series capacitor, shunt inductor, load, grounds, and scope connections.
Run ERC and treat errors as blockers.
Use the generated/internal AC sweep output, not a decorative curve.
Measure normalized cutoff gain and input impedance at fc.
Compare cutoff and impedance against requirements.
analysisRecipe: AC sweep around fc.
Use returned CSV/vector data for graph and report.
Check gain at fc near -3.01 dB normalized to matched passband.
Check input impedance magnitude near z0 at fc for the supported topology.
validationCriteria: ERC passes.
Generated response data exists.
Cutoff gain is near -3.01 dB normalized.
Input impedance meets requested matched value within tolerance.
Graph shown in app is derived from the generated CSV/vector data.
failureModes: using raw source-to-load gain without accounting for source/load divider
claiming validation from a hand-made graph
missing ground or floating instrument node
iterationRules: Change L/C if cutoff misses target.
Report practicality limits if values are unrealistic for the domain.
Implement missing general AC sweep capability for unsupported topologies.
capabilityGaps: Only this matched high-pass has a dedicated synthesis/analysis tool today; general filter synthesis and arbitrary SPICE AC analysis are roadmap capabilities.

provenance.author: Djehuti Electronics Lab seed cookbook
provenance.basis: prototype-supported recipe and standard RLC analysis

text: Recipe: matched 2nd-order RLC high-pass. For target fc and z0, use the app's filter_design_high_pass tool when the request matches this supported topology. It builds source resistor, series capacitor, shunt inductor, load, grounds, and scope. Validate with ERC and actual generated AC sweep CSV. Pass when normalized cutoff gain is about -3.01 dB and input impedance magnitude matches z0. Do not fake the plot. Capability gap: arbitrary filter synthesis/AC sweep is not yet generalized.

title: Non-Inverting Op-Amp Amplifier
purpose: Amplify a voltage signal without inverting polarity while presenting high input impedance.
whenToUse: sensor front ends where high input impedance matters
whenNotToUse: input common-mode exceeds op-amp limits
required bandwidth exceeds gain-bandwidth product
output swing/current exceeds device limits

parameters.rg: resistor from inverting input to reference

designEquations: gain = 1 + Rf/Rg
closed-loop bandwidth approximately GBW/gain
minimum slew rate > 2*pi*fmax*Vpeak
designProcedure: Parse gain, signal range, supply rails, load, and bandwidth requirement.
Select candidate op-amp constraints before component values.
Choose Rg and compute Rf; keep resistor values in a practical noise/bias-current range.
Construct op-amp with rails, feedback network, source, and load.
Run ERC.
Run AC sweep for gain/bandwidth and transient analysis for swing/slew/clipping.
Check common-mode range and output swing against model/device data.
analysisRecipe: AC sweep for closed-loop gain and -3 dB bandwidth.
Transient sine at maximum frequency/amplitude to check slew/clipping.
Operating point to verify bias and output center.
validationCriteria: Gain within tolerance.
Bandwidth meets requirement.
Transient output does not clip or slew-limit.
Input common-mode and output swing stay inside device limits.
iterationRules: Choose a faster op-amp or reduce gain.
Adjust feedback values for bias/noise tradeoff.
Add output isolation or compensation for capacitive load.
capabilityGaps: The prototype needs op-amp symbols/models and general AC/transient SPICE tools before this recipe can be fully executed by the agent.
text: Recipe: non-inverting op-amp amplifier. Gain = 1 + Rf/Rg; closed-loop bandwidth about GBW/gain; slew rate must exceed 2*pi*fmax*Vpeak. Build source, op-amp rails, feedback network, and load. Validate with ERC, operating point, AC sweep, and transient. Capability gap: op-amp models/symbols and general AC/transient tools must be exposed before full autonomous execution.

title: Common-Emitter BJT Voltage Amplifier
purpose: Create an inverting voltage gain stage with controllable bias, gain, and bandwidth.
whenToUse: preamp stages where inversion is acceptable
whenNotToUse: precision gain without feedback
large load current
wide temperature range without bias stabilization
designEquations: choose vceq near vcc/2 for symmetrical swing
re approximately 25mV/Ie at room temperature
small-signal gain with bypassed emitter approximately -Rc/re loaded by output load
unbypassed gain approximately -Rc/(re+Re_ac)
designProcedure: Pick quiescent current and collector voltage swing target.
Choose collector resistor from Vcc, Vceq, and Icq.
Choose emitter resistor for thermal stability and bias point.
Design base divider stiff enough versus base current but not wasteful.
Add coupling capacitors for low-frequency cutoff if AC-coupled.
Run operating point, then AC sweep and transient.
Check clipping and sensitivity to beta variation.
analysisRecipe: Operating point for Ic, Vce, node voltages.
AC sweep for gain/bandwidth.
Transient sine to inspect clipping.
Parameter sweep over beta or resistor tolerance when available.
validationCriteria: Bias point leaves required output swing.
Gain and bandwidth meet target.
Power dissipation within transistor limits.
Design remains acceptable across beta/tolerance assumptions.
iterationRules: Adjust bias divider/current for stable operating point.
Use emitter degeneration or feedback for stability.
Change coupling capacitors for low-frequency response.
capabilityGaps: The prototype needs transistor models, operating-point execution, AC sweep, transient, and parameter sweep tools exposed for full execution.
text: Recipe: common-emitter BJT amplifier. Choose Icq and Vceq near mid-supply, calculate Rc and emitter/bias network, add coupling/bypass caps as needed. Validate operating point, AC gain/bandwidth, transient clipping, power, and beta/tolerance sensitivity. Capability gap: transistor models and general OP/AC/transient/sweep tools must be exposed.

title: Bridge Rectifier with Capacitor-Input Filter
purpose: Convert AC to unregulated DC with full-wave bridge rectification and a reservoir capacitor.
whenNotToUse: isolated mains design without safety model
precision regulation by itself
high power without thermal/inrush checks
designEquations: vpeak approximately VacRms*sqrt(2) minus two diode drops for bridge conduction
ripple approximately Iload/(2*fline*C) for full-wave rectifier
capacitor ripple current and diode surge current must be checked
designProcedure: Define transformer/source RMS voltage, line frequency, load current, allowed ripple, and safety assumptions.
Estimate peak DC and diode drops.
Calculate reservoir capacitance from ripple target.
Select diode voltage/current/surge ratings and capacitor voltage/ripple ratings.
Construct bridge, capacitor, and load.
Run transient analysis for startup and steady-state ripple.
Measure DC average, ripple peak-to-peak, diode current peaks, and capacitor stress.
analysisRecipe: Transient startup for inrush and capacitor charge.
Transient steady-state after settling for ripple and load voltage.
Temperature/load variation where required.
validationCriteria: Average DC voltage and ripple meet requirement.
Diodes and capacitor stay within voltage/current ratings.
Inrush and power dissipation are acceptable.
iterationRules: Increase capacitance, reduce load, or add regulator if ripple too high.
Use higher-rated diodes/capacitor or add inrush limiting if stress is excessive.
capabilityGaps: General diode models, transient execution, and waveform measurements must be exposed before autonomous validation.
text: Recipe: bridge rectifier capacitor-input supply. Vpeak roughly VacRMS*sqrt(2)-two diode drops; full-wave ripple roughly Iload/(2*fline*C). Validate with transient startup and steady-state ripple from actual waveforms, checking diode surge, capacitor voltage/ripple, load voltage, and safety assumptions. Capability gap: general transient/waveform measurement tools are needed.

title: 555 Astable Oscillator
purpose: Generate a free-running square or pulse waveform from a 555 timer and RC timing network.
whenNotToUse: precision clocks
very high frequency
low-power CMOS timing unless using CMOS 555 variant
designEquations: frequency approximately 1.44/((Ra + 2*Rb)*C)
duty cycle approximately (Ra + Rb)/(Ra + 2*Rb) for classic astable
designProcedure: Parse frequency, duty cycle, supply, and output load.
Choose C for practical resistor range.
Solve Ra/Rb; note classic astable duty cycle cannot go below 50 percent without diode or alternate topology.
Build 555 astable with timing capacitor and supply decoupling.
Run transient analysis long enough for multiple cycles.
Measure period, frequency, duty cycle, output high/low levels, and startup.
analysisRecipe: Transient simulation for at least 10 cycles.
Use scope/strip chart for slow oscillators.
Measure threshold capacitor waveform and output waveform.
validationCriteria: Frequency and duty cycle meet tolerance.
Output swing meets load requirement.
Startup occurs and waveform is stable.
failureModes: duty cycle impossible with classic topology
iterationRules: Change C and resistor values.
Use diode-modified topology for duty cycle below 50 percent.
Select CMOS/bipolar 555 model appropriate to load and supply.
capabilityGaps: 555 macro-model, transient solver execution, and automatic waveform metrics are required for full validation.
text: Recipe: 555 astable oscillator. Frequency about 1.44/((Ra+2Rb)C), duty about (Ra+Rb)/(Ra+2Rb). Build timer, timing network, decoupling, and load. Validate with transient data over many cycles; measure frequency, duty, output levels, startup. Classic topology cannot go below 50 percent duty without modification. Capability gap: 555 model/transient/waveform metrics.

title: DMM, Oscilloscope, and Slow Strip-Chart Measurement Workflow
purpose: Choose and configure node-based instruments for numerical, waveform, and slow multi-channel measurements.
whenToUse: record slow drift, ripple envelope, startup, thermal or control behavior
whenNotToUse: when no schematic nodes are assigned
when solver/vector data is required but no analysis has been run
designProcedure: Place instrument nodes on the schematic rather than assuming a fixed bench.
Wire DMM HI/LO and scope channels/reference to explicit circuit nodes.
Open floating instrument panels when the user wants live displays.
For slow behavior, enable strip chart recording and choose per-channel scaling unless comparing absolute amplitudes.
Use ERC to detect floating probes or missing ground before claiming measurement readiness.
analysisRecipe: Use DMM for scalar DC/AC/R measurements.
Use oscilloscope channels for time-domain comparisons.
Use strip chart for slow multi-channel logging or long settling behavior.
Use solver datasets when validation requires simulated numeric evidence.
validationCriteria: Instrument nodes are wired to intended nets.
Channel colors and labels match connections.
Measurement display derives from live instrument state or solver data, not hand-created artifacts.
Recording window and scaling are documented.
failureModes: channel label does not match schematic net
iterationRules: Reconnect probes, rerun ERC, and reopen instrument panel.
Switch scale mode when traces obscure each other or absolute comparison is needed.
capabilityGaps: Instrument panels currently show prototype slow recorder traces; binding strip charts to solver/live datasets is the next reusable capability.
text: Measurement recipe: use node-based DMM and scope instruments. Place and wire DMM HI/LO and scope channel/reference pins explicitly, open floating panels, run ERC, then use DMM for scalar values, scope for waveform comparison, and strip chart for slow multi-channel recording. Current gap: strip charts need binding to solver/live datasets; do not claim data-backed validation from prototype demo traces.

title: Control Loop Frequency-Response Validation
purpose: Validate feedback-loop stability and dynamic performance using calculated or simulated response data.
whenNotToUse: when loop injection point is undefined
when nonlinear startup behavior is the only concern
designProcedure: Define plant, controller, feedback sign, and loop break/injection point.
Derive or simulate loop transfer function.
Generate Bode data from actual calculated/simulated vectors.
Measure crossover, phase margin, gain margin, and bandwidth.
Run step response for time-domain behavior.
Iterate compensation values until stability and transient requirements pass.
analysisRecipe: AC/transfer-function analysis for loop gain.
Step response for overshoot, settling, and steady-state error.
Parameter/load variation for robustness.
validationCriteria: Positive phase and gain margin meet requirement.
Closed-loop bandwidth and step metrics satisfy spec.
Plots are generated from actual calculated/simulated data.
iterationRules: Adjust lead/lag/PID compensation.
Reduce bandwidth if phase margin is too low.
Add model detail when measured behavior differs from simplified transfer function.
capabilityGaps: The prototype needs reusable transfer-function, Bode/Nyquist, step-response, and margin-measurement tools before autonomous control-loop validation.
text: Analysis recipe: control-loop frequency response. Define plant/controller/feedback/injection point, generate Bode data from actual calculated or simulated vectors, measure crossover, phase margin, gain margin, bandwidth, then run step response for overshoot/settling/error. Iterate compensation. Capability gap: transfer-function, Bode/Nyquist, step-response, and margin tools need reusable app exposure.

title: Full-Wave Bridge Rectifier Validation
purpose: Convert an AC input into pulsating or filtered DC using four diodes while checking diode stress and load behavior.
whenNotToUse: very low voltage supplies where diode drops dominate
high efficiency supplies without synchronous rectification
mains-connected circuits without safety/isolation handling
designEquations: vPeak = vacRms * sqrt(2)
bridge output peak approximately vPeak - 2*Vf
ripple frequency is 2*line frequency for full-wave rectification
diode PIV rating must exceed reverse voltage with margin
designProcedure: Parse AC input, load, allowed ripple, and stress limits.
Select diode current, surge, and reverse-voltage ratings.
Construct bridge and load; add capacitor filter only if requested.
Run ERC before simulation.
Run transient analysis for several line cycles.
Measure output average, ripple, diode current peaks, and reverse voltage.
analysisRecipe: Transient startup for surge current.
Transient steady-state for average DC and ripple.
Worst-case input/load sweep when ratings matter.
validationCriteria: Output voltage and ripple meet requirement.
Diode current, surge, power, and reverse voltage stay within ratings.
Waveform evidence comes from transient simulation or instrument dataset.
iterationRules: Use Schottky or synchronous rectification for low-voltage efficiency.
Increase diode/capacitor ratings or add inrush limiting for stress failures.
Add regulator/filtering when ripple is excessive.
capabilityGaps: The prototype still needs general diode models, transient solver execution, and automatic waveform metrics exposed as reusable tools.
text: Recipe: full-wave bridge rectifier. Estimate bridge peak output as VacRMS*sqrt(2)-2 diode drops, ripple at twice line frequency when filtered, and diode PIV/current/surge ratings. Validate with transient data over startup and steady-state, measuring output, ripple, diode current, and reverse voltage. Capability gap: general diode transient tooling and waveform measurements are not fully exposed.

title: Continuous-Conduction Buck Converter First Pass
purpose: Step down a DC input to a lower regulated output using a switching stage, inductor, output capacitor, and control loop.
whenToUse: battery or bus conversion where linear dissipation is excessive
whenNotToUse: when EMI/switching noise cannot be tolerated
when isolation is required
when load is tiny and a linear regulator is simpler
designEquations: ideal duty D = Vout/Vin
inductor L approximately (Vin - Vout)*D/(deltaI*fsw)
output capacitor from ripple and transient targets
switch and diode stresses depend on Vin, Iout, ripple, and topology
designProcedure: Parse voltage range, load, ripple, efficiency, transient, and EMI requirements.
Choose switching frequency and ripple fraction.
Calculate duty range and inductor value.
Select capacitor value/ESR and switch/diode current-voltage ratings.
Construct power stage and controller model.
Run transient startup and load-step simulations.
Run loop analysis when feedback compensation is present.
analysisRecipe: Transient switching simulation for ripple and startup.
Load-step transient for regulation.
AC loop gain for compensated designs.
Loss and thermal estimates for switch, diode, inductor, and capacitor.
validationCriteria: Output voltage, ripple, and transient response meet spec across Vin/load.
Inductor current remains in intended conduction mode.
Switch, diode, capacitor, and inductor stress stay within ratings.
Loop stability margins meet requirement when closed-loop.
iterationRules: Adjust L/C/fsw/ripple targets.
Change topology or synchronous rectification for efficiency.
Add compensation or reduce bandwidth for stability.
capabilityGaps: The prototype needs switch models, PWM/controller primitives, transient solver performance, loss estimation, and loop-gain tools before autonomous buck validation.
text: Recipe: CCM buck converter. Ideal duty D=Vout/Vin; L roughly (Vin-Vout)*D/(deltaI*fsw). Select switch/diode/inductor/capacitor by ripple, stress, loss, and transient requirements. Validate startup, ripple, load step, losses, thermal, and loop stability from actual simulation data. Capability gap: switching primitives, controller models, loss estimates, and loop-gain tools are needed.

title: Simple Zener Voltage Reference
purpose: Generate a simple shunt voltage reference using a resistor-biased Zener diode.
whenToUse: simple regulator references with modest precision
whenNotToUse: precision low-noise references
low-current battery systems
wide temperature accuracy requirements without compensation
designEquations: series resistor R = (Vin - Vz)/(Iz + Iload)
check Iz at VinMin with max load and at VinMax with min load
zener power Pz = Vz * Iz
designProcedure: Parse input range, reference voltage, load current, accuracy, temperature, and noise requirements.
Select zener voltage/current region and power rating.
Choose series resistor so zener remains in regulation at worst low input/high load and below power limit at high input/low load.
Construct source, resistor, zener, and load.
Run DC operating point and DC sweep over Vin/load.
Check temperature/noise only if models support it.
analysisRecipe: Operating point at nominal conditions.
DC sweep over input voltage and load current.
Power calculation for zener and resistor.
Temperature sweep when supported.
validationCriteria: Reference voltage stays within allowed range.
Zener current remains between minimum regulation and maximum rating.
Power and thermal limits are respected.
iterationRules: Adjust series resistor or choose higher power zener.
Add buffer or use bandgap/reference IC for precision/load current.
Add filtering if noise is excessive.
capabilityGaps: DC sweep, load sweep, temperature sweep, and zener model handling need reusable agent tools for full validation.
text: Recipe: simple Zener reference. Choose series resistor so zener current stays in regulation at low Vin/high load and below power at high Vin/low load; Pz=Vz*Iz. Validate with operating point and DC sweeps over input/load, plus temperature/noise where modeled. Capability gap: DC/load/temp sweeps and zener model handling need reusable tools.

title: Common-Source FET Voltage Amplifier
purpose: Create an inverting voltage gain stage with high input impedance using a FET device.
whenNotToUse: precision gain without feedback
large process variation without bias control
load current beyond device limits
designEquations: small-signal gain approximately -gm*(Rd || load) with bypassed source degeneration
source degeneration reduces gain and improves bias stability
bias point depends strongly on selected FET model
designProcedure: Select FET family/model appropriate to signal range and noise needs.
Choose drain current and voltage swing target.
Set drain/source resistor or current source for bias point.
Add gate bias/reference and input coupling as needed.
Run operating point, AC sweep, and transient.
Check clipping, device region, gain, input impedance, and sensitivity to device variation.
analysisRecipe: Operating point to verify region and bias.
AC sweep for gain and bandwidth.
Transient for clipping and large-signal behavior.
Parameter sweep for threshold/Idss variation where possible.
validationCriteria: Device remains in intended operating region.
Gain/bandwidth/input impedance meet requirements.
Output swing remains unclipped across expected variation.
iterationRules: Add source degeneration or current-source bias for stability.
Choose a different FET/model for noise, gm, or swing.
Adjust coupling/bypass capacitors for bandwidth.
capabilityGaps: FET symbols/models, operating-point, AC, transient, and parameter sweep tools are required for full autonomous execution.
text: Recipe: common-source FET amplifier. Pick FET model, bias current, drain/source network, and load; approximate gain as -gm*(Rd||load), modified by source degeneration. Validate bias region, gain, bandwidth, input impedance, clipping, and device variation. Capability gap: FET models and OP/AC/transient/sweep tools are needed.

title: Complementary Class AB Output Stage
purpose: Drive a low-impedance load with a complementary output stage while reducing crossover distortion versus Class B.
whenToUse: linear load drivers needing bidirectional current
whenNotToUse: maximum efficiency applications where Class D is preferred
loads outside safe operating area
designs lacking thermal protection
designEquations: Pout = Vrms^2 / Rload
device dissipation depends on output power, rail voltage, load, and conduction angle
bias voltage must track device temperature to avoid thermal runaway
designProcedure: Parse load, output power, supply rails, distortion, efficiency, and thermal requirements.
Calculate required output voltage/current swing.
Select output devices and emitter/source resistors.
Design bias network and thermal tracking.
Construct stage with load and protection elements.
Run transient sine tests at small and rated output.
Estimate dissipation and safe operating area.
Check stability with reactive/capacitive load models.
analysisRecipe: Operating point for quiescent current.
Transient sine for clipping and crossover distortion.
Fourier/distortion analysis where available.
Thermal and load-stability checks.
validationCriteria: Output power target met without clipping.
Quiescent current stable and thermally safe.
Distortion/load stability meet requirement.
Device voltage/current/power within safe operating area.
iterationRules: Adjust bias and emitter/source resistors.
Increase rail/device ratings or reduce output power.
Add output network/protection/compensation for load stability.
capabilityGaps: Power transistor models, distortion analysis, thermal/SOA calculation, and reactive-load stability tools are needed for full validation.
text: Recipe: complementary Class AB output stage. Compute output voltage/current from power and load, design bias/thermal tracking and emitter/source resistors, then validate quiescent current, clipping, crossover distortion, dissipation, SOA, and reactive-load stability from actual data. Capability gap: power models, distortion, thermal/SOA, and stability tools.

title: Wien Bridge Sine Oscillator
purpose: Generate a low-distortion sine wave using a Wien bridge frequency-selective network and amplitude stabilization.
whenNotToUse: precision frequency reference
wide tuning range without tracking components
very low distortion without proven amplitude control
designEquations: f0 = 1/(2*pi*R*C) for equal R and C Wien network
oscillation requires loop gain slightly greater than 1 at startup and near 1 at steady state
amplifier closed-loop gain nominally 3 for sustained oscillation
designProcedure: Parse frequency, amplitude, supply rails, and distortion requirement.
Choose R/C values for f0.
Design gain stage and amplitude-control element.
Run transient analysis long enough for startup and settling.
Measure frequency, amplitude, startup time, steady-state distortion, and clipping.
Iterate gain/amplitude control if startup fails or distortion is high.
analysisRecipe: Transient startup and steady-state waveform.
Fourier/distortion analysis after settling.
Parameter sweep for gain margin and amplitude-control robustness.
validationCriteria: Oscillation starts reliably.
Steady-state frequency and amplitude meet spec.
Clipping/distortion within requirement.
Amplitude control stabilizes rather than grows/decays.
failureModes: loop gain too low for startup
loop gain too high causing clipping
iterationRules: Adjust gain slightly above startup threshold.
Improve amplitude control or choose op-amp with adequate bandwidth/slew rate.
Tune R/C values and rerun transient.
capabilityGaps: Op-amp models, transient startup, Fourier/distortion metrics, and oscillator-specific measurements are needed for full autonomous validation.
text: Recipe: Wien bridge sine oscillator. For equal R/C, f0=1/(2*pi*R*C); amplifier gain nominally 3 with amplitude stabilization. Validate startup, settling, frequency, amplitude, clipping, and distortion from transient/Fourier data. Capability gap: op-amp models, transient startup, and distortion metrics.

title: Comparator-Integrator Triangle Wave Generator
purpose: Generate square and triangle waves using a Schmitt trigger/comparator that drives an integrator.
whenNotToUse: precision waveform synthesis requiring DDS
high frequency beyond op-amp/comparator slew/bandwidth
rail-limited supplies that cannot support desired amplitude
designEquations: integrator slope = Vin/(R*C)
period is set by threshold span divided by integrator slope
frequency depends on comparator output amplitude, R, C, and hysteresis thresholds
designProcedure: Define amplitude, frequency, rails, and load.
Set Schmitt thresholds for desired triangle amplitude.
Choose integrator R/C from required slope and comparator output swing.
Construct comparator and integrator loop.
Run transient simulation for startup and several cycles.
Measure frequency, amplitude, duty cycle, slew limits, and clipping.
analysisRecipe: Transient waveform simulation.
Scope channels for square and triangle outputs.
Fourier or distortion analysis only if waveform purity matters.
validationCriteria: Triangle amplitude and frequency meet requirement.
Square wave duty/levels acceptable.
No slew-rate or output swing violation.
Waveform data comes from transient results.
iterationRules: Change R/C or thresholds for frequency/amplitude.
Choose faster devices or lower amplitude/frequency.
Add reset/limiting if integrator saturates.
capabilityGaps: Comparator/op-amp models, transient solver, and automatic waveform metrics are needed for full execution.
text: Recipe: comparator-integrator triangle generator. Schmitt thresholds set triangle amplitude; integrator slope equals Vin/(R*C), so period follows threshold span divided by slope. Validate transient square/triangle waveforms, frequency, amplitude, duty, slew, and clipping. Capability gap: comparator/op-amp models and waveform metrics.

title: Schmitt Trigger Threshold Detector
purpose: Convert a noisy or slowly changing analog input into a clean logic-level output using separate rising and falling thresholds.
whenNotToUse: precision ADC replacement
inputs outside common-mode range
signals requiring no hysteresis
designEquations: thresholds derive from resistor divider including output feedback state
hysteresis = rising threshold - falling threshold
check input common-mode and output level compatibility
designProcedure: Parse thresholds, input range/noise, output logic levels, and supply rails.
Choose comparator and reference compatible with input common-mode and output needs.
Calculate feedback divider for rising/falling thresholds.
Construct comparator, reference, and feedback network.
Run DC sweep or transient ramp through thresholds.
Measure switching points and output levels.
analysisRecipe: DC sweep input through threshold range.
Transient ramp or noisy input to confirm clean switching.
Load/output level check.
validationCriteria: Measured rising/falling thresholds match spec.
Output levels compatible with receiving circuit.
No chatter for expected noise amplitude.
Device input/output limits respected.
iterationRules: Adjust feedback resistor ratio or reference.
Select comparator with suitable input/output range.
Increase hysteresis or add input filtering for noise.

whenNotToUse: safety-critical thermal shutdown without independent protection
systems needing accurate thermal modeling but no sensor placement data
fans with unknown startup/stall behavior
designProcedure: Parse thermal target, sensor type/location, fan voltage/current, acoustic constraints, and fault behavior.
Choose on/off hysteresis or proportional PWM control.
Design sensor interface and thresholds/curve.
Select driver for fan startup current and flyback if inductive.
Run electrical transient and control response with thermal profile input.
Validate thresholds, hysteresis, startup, and fault behavior.
analysisRecipe: DC threshold sweep for sensor network.
Transient temperature ramp for fan control behavior.
Driver current/thermal check for startup and PWM.
Closed-loop thermal model when available.
validationCriteria: Fan turns on/off or modulates at intended temperatures.
Hysteresis prevents chatter.
Driver survives startup/PWM current.
Sensor placement and thermal assumptions documented.
failureModes: sensor not coupled to heat source
iterationRules: Adjust hysteresis/curve and sensor network.
Use stronger driver or fan tach feedback.
Add independent thermal shutdown for safety.
capabilityGaps: Thermal plant models, fan models, thermistor tolerance sweeps, and temperature-profile simulation need reusable support.
text: Recipe: fan controller. Use thermistor/sensor thresholds, hysteresis or PWM curve, and a driver sized for startup current; validate threshold sweep, temperature-ramp behavior, chatter immunity, driver stress, and thermal assumptions. Capability gap: thermal/fan models and temperature profile simulation.

title: Constant-Current LED Driver
purpose: Drive LEDs at a controlled current while checking voltage headroom, dimming, and thermal limits.
whenNotToUse: simple low-current indicators where resistor is sufficient
strings exceeding compliance voltage
thermal path unknown for high-power LEDs
designProcedure: Parse LED current, string voltage, supply range, dimming, efficiency, and thermal requirements.
Choose linear or switching current regulator based on headroom and dissipation.
Calculate sense resistor and compliance voltage.
Construct LED string and driver.
Run operating point and supply/temperature/load sweeps.
Validate current accuracy, dissipation, dimming behavior, and thermal margin.
analysisRecipe: Operating point for LED current and voltages.
DC sweep over supply and LED Vf tolerance.
Transient PWM dimming if applicable.
Thermal power estimate for LED and driver.
validationCriteria: LED current within target over supply/Vf range.
Driver has enough compliance without overheating.
Dimming behavior meets requirement.
LED thermal limits respected.
iterationRules: Use switching driver for efficiency/headroom.
Change string length or supply voltage.
Add thermal foldback or heat sinking.
capabilityGaps: LED electrothermal models, dimming metrics, supply/Vf sweeps, and thermal tools need reusable support.
text: Recipe: constant-current LED driver. Choose linear or switching regulator, calculate sense resistor and compliance, then validate current over supply/Vf range, dimming, dissipation, and LED thermal margin. Capability gap: LED electrothermal models, dimming metrics, sweeps, and thermal tools.

title: Common-Mode Choke Selection and Validation
purpose: Use a common-mode choke to attenuate common-mode noise while passing desired differential current.
whenNotToUse: differential-mode noise without additional filter elements
DC current above choke rating
signals where leakage inductance distorts normal operation
designProcedure: Parse noise mode/frequency, normal current, safety/leakage constraints, and signal bandwidth.
Select choke impedance/current/saturation and winding insulation ratings.
Combine with capacitors/damping as needed for filter topology.
Construct equivalent model with common-mode and differential parasitics.
Run AC/noise attenuation estimate and current stress checks.
Validate normal signal/power behavior and saturation margin.
analysisRecipe: Common-mode AC attenuation estimate.
Differential-mode insertion loss check.
Current/saturation and thermal estimate.
EMI/return-path review.
validationCriteria: Common-mode attenuation meets target band.
Normal differential current and signal not degraded excessively.
Choke not saturated or overheated.
Safety insulation/leakage assumptions respected.
iterationRules: Add differential filter or damping.
Choose higher current/lower capacitance choke.
Revise grounding/shielding return paths.
capabilityGaps: Coupled inductor/choke models, common-vs-differential analysis, EMI spectra, and safety capacitor checks need reusable support.
text: Recipe: common-mode choke. Select impedance over noise band, current/saturation, leakage, and insulation; validate common-mode attenuation, differential insertion loss, current/thermal margin, and safety/leakage assumptions. Capability gap: coupled magnetic models, CM/DM analysis, EMI spectra, and safety checks.

title: Conducted EMI Input Filter Workflow
purpose: Reduce conducted emissions or susceptibility with common-mode and differential-mode input filtering.
whenNotToUse: radiated problems caused mainly by layout loops
safety-critical mains filter without compliance review
filters that destabilize upstream/downstream converters
designProcedure: Identify common-mode versus differential-mode noise path and frequency range.
Choose filter topology and component ratings/current/leakage.
Add damping if source/load can resonate with filter.
Construct equivalent source-filter-load model.
Run AC attenuation and transient/inrush checks.
Validate converter stability and normal operation with filter inserted.
analysisRecipe: AC insertion-loss estimate for DM and CM paths.
Transient inrush and startup interaction.
Stability check for converter input impedance interaction.
Layout/current-loop review.
validationCriteria: Attenuation target met in noise band.
Normal current/voltage drop/thermal acceptable.
No unstable input-filter interaction.
Safety leakage and capacitor ratings acceptable.
iterationRules: Separate CM and DM filter paths.
Add damping or change corner frequency.
Improve layout and shield/return termination.
capabilityGaps: EMI spectra, CM/DM separation, insertion-loss tooling, converter input impedance, and layout loop checks need reusable support.
text: Recipe: conducted EMI input filter. Identify CM versus DM paths, choose filter elements and damping, and validate insertion loss, inrush, converter stability, current/thermal, leakage, and layout. Capability gap: EMI spectra, CM/DM tools, insertion loss, converter impedance, and layout checks.

title: Grounding and Return-Current Review
purpose: Plan and validate ground/reference connections so signal, power, shield, and chassis currents do not corrupt measurements or create unsafe paths.
whenNotToUse: as a slogan replacing return-current analysis
when safety earth/chassis requirements are unknown
when PCB/layout current paths are unavailable
designProcedure: Identify all current loops and return paths by frequency and magnitude.
Separate high-current/noisy returns from sensitive references until intentional joining point.
Define chassis/shield/earth strategy and isolation boundaries.
Use ERC/net labels to catch accidental shorts or floating references.
Review PCB current paths, not only schematic names.
Validate noise injection or ground offset effects when models exist.
analysisRecipe: Schematic net/domain review.
Ground-loop and return-current path review.
Noise injection/common-mode sensitivity simulation where possible.
PCB layout review for actual current paths.
validationCriteria: Every signal has an intentional return path.
No high-current return shares sensitive impedance unintentionally.
Shield/chassis/earth strategy documented.
Isolation and safety boundaries not accidentally bridged.
failureModes: star ground used without loop analysis
iterationRules: Move join point or split domains with net ties/isolation.
Add Kelvin sensing or differential measurement.
Revise PCB return paths and shield terminations.
capabilityGaps: Return-current visualization, domain-aware ERC, PCB/layout extraction, and noise-injection analysis need reusable tool support.
text: Recipe: grounding review. Identify current loops/returns, noisy versus sensitive domains, shield/chassis/earth policy, isolation boundaries, and PCB return paths. Validate with ERC/domain review and noise/offset simulation when available. Capability gap: return-current visualization, domain-aware ERC, layout extraction, and noise injection.

title: Source Termination for Fast Digital Lines
purpose: Reduce reflections on a point-to-point line by matching source impedance plus series resistor to line characteristic impedance.
whenToUse: fast edges on PCB traces or cables
source-end damping where DC power loss must be low
whenNotToUse: multi-drop buses without topology analysis
very long lines needing receiver/parallel termination
unknown line impedance or edge rate
designProcedure: Determine whether line delay is significant versus edge rate.
Estimate or measure line impedance Z0 and driver output impedance.
Choose series resistor so Rsource + Rseries approximates Z0.
Construct driver, line, receiver, and load model.
Run transient edge simulation at receiver.
Measure overshoot, undershoot, settling, and timing margin.
analysisRecipe: Transmission-line transient reflection simulation.
Parameter sweep over resistor value and load capacitance.
Eye/timing check for repeated data if needed.
validationCriteria: Receiver waveform crosses thresholds cleanly.
Overshoot/undershoot within device ratings.
Settling occurs before sampling time.
Termination value robust to tolerance/layout variation.
failureModes: series resistor too far from driver
iterationRules: Adjust resistor value or topology.
Use parallel/AC termination or controlled impedance routing.
Reduce edge rate or improve layout.
capabilityGaps: Transmission-line elements, reflection/eye metrics, controlled-impedance metadata, and layout-aware stubs need reusable support.
text: Recipe: source termination. If line delay matters versus edge rate, set driver impedance plus series resistor near Z0 and validate receiver waveform, overshoot, settling, and timing from transmission-line transient data. Capability gap: transmission-line models, reflection/eye metrics, impedance metadata, and layout-aware stubs.

title: PCB Decoupling and Return-Path Review
purpose: Translate schematic intent into PCB placement/routing checks for decoupling, return current, power integrity, and sensitive nodes.
whenNotToUse: as proof without actual layout data
when package/pinout/current paths are unknown
as replacement for EMI or SI simulation when required

parameters.returnPath: plane/path under signal or power loop

designProcedure: Identify IC/load current spectra and sensitive nodes.
Assign local decoupling close to power pins with short return loop.
Plan bulk capacitance and power distribution path.
Keep return paths under signals and away from sensitive references.
Review high-current and switching loops for area and coupling.
Validate with layout extraction or checklist until tools exist.
analysisRecipe: Schematic-to-layout checklist for decoupling placement.
PDN impedance estimate where models exist.
Return-current and loop-area review.
Thermal/current density review for high-current paths.
validationCriteria: Each active IC/load has appropriate local decoupling path.
High di/dt loops are small and routed deliberately.
Sensitive nodes shielded/guarded/kept away from noisy returns.
Power and thermal paths meet current requirements.
failureModes: capacitor value present but placed far away
return path cut by split plane
sensitive node routed near noisy current
iterationRules: Move capacitors and vias close to pins.
Re-route returns and reduce loop area.
Add guard/partitioning/thermal copper as needed.
capabilityGaps: PCB layout import, placement-rule checks, PDN impedance, loop-area visualization, and current/thermal extraction need reusable support.
text: Recipe: PCB decoupling and return-path review. Check local decoupling placement/loop area, bulk capacitance, return paths, sensitive nodes, switching loops, power/current and thermal routing. Capability gap: layout import, placement checks, PDN impedance, loop visualization, and extraction tools.

title: SPICE AC Sweep Validation Procedure
purpose: Run and interpret small-signal AC sweep data from the actual circuit model rather than producing decorative plots.
whenNotToUse: large-signal clipping or startup behavior
oscillators requiring transient startup
switching ripple requiring time-domain analysis
designProcedure: Run ERC and fix errors before analysis.
Configure AC source amplitude and sweep range around expected features.
Run SPICE AC analysis and capture numeric vectors.
Compute gain/phase/impedance from returned vectors.
Measure cutoff, peak, bandwidth, rolloff, or margins as required.
Generate plots only from returned vectors and cite result paths.
analysisRecipe: AC sweep vector retrieval.
Derived measurements from numeric vectors.
Plot generation from CSV/vector data.
Comparison against requirement tolerance.
validationCriteria: ERC passes or warnings are explained.
Sweep range/resolution covers requirement.
Metrics are calculated from solver vectors.
Plot and conclusion cite actual generated data.
failureModes: linear analysis used for nonlinear large-signal claim
iterationRules: Adjust sweep range/resolution and rerun.
Fix source/probe/reference.
Switch to transient/noise/etc. if AC assumptions do not apply.
capabilityGaps: General arbitrary-circuit SPICE run, vector retrieval, expression measurements, and plot panels need fuller reusable tool exposure.
text: Recipe: SPICE AC sweep. Run ERC, configure AC source and sweep, run solver, retrieve numeric vectors, calculate gain/phase/cutoff/bandwidth/rolloff/margins, and plot only from solver data. Capability gap: arbitrary-circuit SPICE execution, vector retrieval, expressions, and plot panels need fuller exposure.

title: Systematic Bias and Connectivity Fault Diagnosis
purpose: Diagnose why a circuit misses expected operating behavior by separating connectivity, bias, loading, saturation, and wrong-value faults.
whenNotToUse: before inspecting the current circuit model
when result was not produced by actual tool data
as a substitute for component/model validation
designProcedure: Inspect authoritative circuit model and recipe expectations.
Run ERC and resolve errors first.
Compare operating point or measured nodes against expected bias.
Check opens, shorts, wrong values/units, missing ground, and load/reference errors.
Use targeted sweeps or substitutions to isolate sensitivity.
Modify one cause at a time and rerun validation.
analysisRecipe: ERC review.
Operating point comparison where available.
Targeted parameter sweep or component substitution.
Instrument/probe connection verification.
validationCriteria: Root cause tied to a concrete model/tool observation.
Fix changes the failing metric in the expected direction.
Rerun validation demonstrates requirement pass or a remaining blocker.
iterationRules: Narrow with model inspection and targeted measurement.
Repair connectivity/value/model issue.
Rerun the original acceptance analysis after each fix.
capabilityGaps: Structured diff of circuit revisions, operating-point probes, parameter sweep, and failure-class classifiers need reusable support.
text: Recipe: fault diagnosis. Inspect model, run ERC, compare expected and actual bias/measurements, check opens/shorts/wrong values/grounds/loading/saturation, isolate with targeted sweeps, change one cause, and rerun validation. Capability gap: revision diff, operating-point probes, parameter sweeps, and failure classifiers.

title: Nominal, Tolerance, Supply, and Load Verification Plan
purpose: Turn a design requirement into a verification matrix covering nominal operation and expected variations.
whenToUse: before claiming a design satisfies requirements
when tolerances, temperature, supply, load, startup, or fault behavior matter
whenNotToUse: as a replacement for domain-specific safety/certification
when no requirement tolerances are defined
when underlying simulation models are not credible
designProcedure: Translate requirement into measurable metrics and tolerances.
Run nominal validation first and save evidence.
Define variation axes: component tolerance, supply, load, input, temperature, startup/shutdown, and fault cases.
Run sweeps/Monte Carlo/worst-case analyses where tools exist.
Compare every metric against pass/fail limits and record evidence paths.
Report unmet requirements as failures or capability gaps, not success.
analysisRecipe: Nominal simulation/measurement.
Parameter, supply, load, input, and temperature sweeps.
Monte Carlo or worst-case analysis when supported.
Evidence report with artifact paths.
validationCriteria: Every requirement maps to at least one metric.
Nominal and required variation cases pass.
Evidence paths point to actual tool outputs.
Unverified cases are explicitly listed.
iterationRules: Add missing measurement/tool capability.
Adjust design and rerun full matrix.
Record residual risk when model coverage is incomplete.
capabilityGaps: General sweep/Monte Carlo/worst-case runner, metrics engine, and evidence report generator need reusable app tooling.
text: Recipe: design verification matrix. Map requirements to metrics, run nominal evidence, define tolerance/supply/load/input/temp/startup/fault cases, run sweeps or Monte Carlo where supported, and report pass/fail with artifact paths. Capability gap: sweep/Monte Carlo/worst-case runner, metrics engine, and evidence report generator.

Check live tool manifest/cards for an actual tool or instrument path.
If available, use the tool and cite returned evidence.
If unavailable, record a capability gap with general reusable tool needed.
Do not complete the engineering claim by doing hidden work outside the app.
After implementing a new tool, retry the original recipe step.
analysisRecipe: Tool-manifest inspection.
Recipe-to-tool mapping.
Evidence trace review.
Capability gap classification.
validationCriteria: Every engineering claim has either tool evidence or explicit gap.
No graph/result is fabricated outside tool data.
New tools are reusable and documented in cards/manifest.
Original goal is retried after gap closure.

one-off hack instead of reusable capability

when existing tool already provides evidence
for one-off demo shortcuts

Retry the original engineering goal and validate with produced evidence.

without inspecting tool traces and evidence artifacts
